Getting Started¶

Stars, Quasars, and Galaxies! All large luminous bodies in space! How do we classify them? I will use classification methods to try and classify them in this notebook.


What are stars, quasars, and galaxies? Let's look at Wikipedia for a quick introduction on what these objects are.


Stars: "An astronomical object comprising a luminous spheroid of plasma held together by its own gravity." (About Stars)

Quasar: "An extremely luminous active galactic nucleus (AGN), powered by a supermassive black hole, with mass ranging from millions to tens of billions of solar masses, surrounded by a gaseous accretion disc." (About Quasars)

Galaxy: "A gravitationally bound system of stars, stellar remnants, interstellar gas, dust, and dark matter." (About Galaxies)

Before starting any sort of processing on our data, we need to import all of the libraries we will use as well as setting up the environment.

Here is the key for each column in the data set listed on the dataset's kaggle page:


  1. obj_ID = Object Identifier, the unique value that identifies the object in the image catalog used by the CAS
  2. alpha = Right Ascension angle (at J2000 epoch)
  3. delta = Declination angle (at J2000 epoch)
  4. u = Ultraviolet filter in the photometric system
  5. g = Green filter in the photometric system
  6. r = Red filter in the photometric system
  7. i = Near Infrared filter in the photometric system
  8. z = Infrared filter in the photometric system
  9. run_ID = Run Number used to identify the specific scan
  10. rereun_ID = Rerun Number to specify how the image was processed
  11. cam_col = Camera column to identify the scanline within the run
  12. field_ID = Field number to identify each field
  13. spec_obj_ID = Unique ID used for optical spectroscopic objects (this means that 2 different observations with the same spec_obj_ID must share the output class)
  14. class = object class (galaxy, star or quasar object)
  15. redshift = redshift value based on the increase in wavelength
  16. plate = plate ID, identifies each plate in SDSS
  17. MJD = Modified Julian Date, used to indicate when a given piece of SDSS data was taken
  18. fiber_ID = fiber ID that identifies the fiber that pointed the light at the focal plane in each observation

We can see that our data is all over the place in terms of min and max values. We need to standardize our data in order to not bias the model.

In [ ]:
'''
https://towardsdatascience.com/scale-standardize-or-normalize-with-scikit-learn-6ccc7d176a02
https://www.kaggle.com/discdiver/guide-to-scaling-and-standardizing

Standardize data using scikit learn min max scaler
Scikit Learn's min max scaler puts all values between 0 and 1
'''
mm_scaler = MinMaxScaler()
df_classes = df['class']
df_values = df[['alpha', 'delta', 'u', 'g', 'r', 'i', 'z', 'spec_obj_ID', 'redshift']]

col_names = list(df_values.columns)
df_mm = mm_scaler.fit_transform(df_values)
df_mm = pd.DataFrame(df_mm, columns=col_names)

df = pd.concat([df_classes, df_mm], axis=1)

We have gotten data that is not necessary for classification. Finally, it is time to check for imbalances in the amount of data points we have for a given class and encode their names.

In [ ]:
label_encoder = LabelEncoder()
df['class'] = label_encoder.fit_transform(df['class'])

Training¶

We need to seperate our data and apply it to different models and balance out our data. As seen above, our data is extremely unbalanced! We need to rebalance it before training and testing.

In [ ]:
'''
We are going to rebalance our data by oversampling the smaller classes.
This code is from an article on rebalancing imbalanced data

https://towardsdatascience.com/methods-for-dealing-with-imbalanced-data-5b761be45a18
'''
from sklearn.utils import resample

# Separate input features and target
x = df.drop(['class'], axis=1)
y = df['class']

# setting up testing and training sets
xtrain, xtest, ytrain, ytest = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.80)

# concatenate our training data back together
X = pd.concat([xtrain, ytrain], axis=1)

# separate minority and majority classes
galaxy = X[X['class'] == 0]
quasar = X[X['class'] == 1]
star = X[X['class'] == 2]

# upsample minority clases
upsampled_quasar = resample(quasar, replace=True, # sample with replacement
                            n_samples=len(galaxy)) # match number in majority class

upsampled_star = resample(star, replace=True, # sample with replacement
                          n_samples=len(galaxy)) # match number in majority class
  
# combine majority and upsampled minority
upsampled = pd.concat([galaxy, upsampled_quasar, upsampled_star])

# check new class counts
count_plot_new = sns.countplot(upsampled["class"], palette="mako")
plt.title("Class Count",fontsize=20)
count_plot_new.set_ylabel("Count", fontsize = 20)
count_plot_new.set_xlabel("Class (0 = Galaxy, 1 = Quasar, 2 = Star)", fontsize = 20)

Now that the data is split for training and later testing. We can fit it to our models.

In [ ]:
'''
Create our models

Code for creating the models is from Scikit-Learn demo (on canvas), 
Scikit-Learn Cheat Sheet (on canvas), and from Scikit-Learn documentation

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier.html
'''
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

# Create our models
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier()
svc = SVC(kernel='linear')
gnb = GaussianNB()
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=int(m.sqrt(xtrain.shape[0])))
clf = RandomForestClassifier()

Here are the classification algorithms we will be using on our data. Here is the list of algorithms I am using:

  • Decision Tree (tree)

    A decision tree is an algorithm that tries to classify data based on a tree of conditional statements. Typically, the conditional statements yield true or false value and change how the data will branch through the rest of the tree.

  • Support Vector Machine (svc)

    A Support Vector Machine, commonly abbreviated to SVM, is an algorithm that tries to find a hyperplane that can distinguish between different data classes/labels. The Hyperplane is a plane within a N-dimensional space, where N is the number of features of a data point in a given data set.

  • Naive Bayes (gnb)

    Naive Bayes works is a classification algorithm that uses Bayes theorem to classify data. Naive Bayes classifies data using Bayes theorem by estimating the likelibood of a class/label for a given data point.

  • K-Nearest Neighbors (knn)

    K-Nearest Neighbors is an algorithm that classifies piece of data by nearest neighbors' classes. The "K" in K-Nearest Neighbors tells us how many neighbors to look at around our data point.

  • Random Forest (clf)

    Random Forest is an algorithm that uses multiple decision trees to classify a data point. Once a piece of data is ran through the trees, the class predicted by each tree is tallied. The class/label with the highest count is the predicted class for the data point.

For Random forest, I chose to go with the integer result of the square root of the size of the training data: int(m.sqrt(xtrain.shape[0]))

According to this article, the best K size is the square root of N, where N is the number of samples in the training dataset. Adapting this to my code, we can use the statement above to get the same result.

In [ ]:
# Fit our data to the models
tree.fit(xtrain, ytrain)
svc.fit(xtrain, ytrain)
gnb.fit(xtrain, ytrain)
knn.fit(xtrain, ytrain)
clf.fit(xtrain, ytrain)
Out[ ]:
RandomForestClassifier()

Testing and Analysis¶

We have split the data and selected the models to test against our data. My hypothesis is that the K-Nearest Neighbors will be the best algorithm due to the fact that it creates clusters. Because we have three different classes in the data, I believe that the KNN algorithm will be able to create distinct clusters to accurately predict the class of each datapoint

In [ ]:
# Import Metrics
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# Run our tests
y_prediction_tree = tree.predict(xtest)
y_prediction_svc = svc.predict(xtest)
y_prediction_gnb = gnb.predict(xtest)
y_prediction_knn = knn.predict(xtest)
y_prediction_clf = clf.predict(xtest)

# Compile the Accuracy Scores into dataframe
labels = ['Decision Tree', 'Support Vector Machine', 'Naive Bayes', 'K-Nearest Neighbors', 'Random Forest']

scores = []

scores.append(accuracy_score(ytest, y_prediction_tree))
scores.append(accuracy_score(ytest, y_prediction_svc))
scores.append(accuracy_score(ytest, y_prediction_gnb))
scores.append(accuracy_score(ytest, y_prediction_knn))
scores.append(accuracy_score(ytest, y_prediction_clf))

# Code for combining lists into dataframe from Geeks For Geeks
# https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/create-a-pandas-dataframe-from-lists/
accuracy_scores = pd.DataFrame(list(zip(labels, scores)), 
                               columns=['algorithm', 'accuracy'])

# Generate chart
accuracy_chart = sns.barplot(data=accuracy_scores, x='algorithm', y='accuracy', palette="mako")
accuracy_chart.set_xlabel("Algorithm Name", fontsize = 20)
accuracy_chart.set_ylabel("Accuracy [0.0, 1.0]", fontsize = 20)
accuracy_chart.set_title("Accuray of Classification Algorithms on Stellar Objects", fontsize = 20)
accuracy_chart.set(ylim=(0, 1))
Out[ ]:
[(0.0, 1.0)]

Not only was my hypothesis was wrong, it was the lowest performing algorithm in terms of accuracy. Let's look at the confusion matrix for each algorithm as well as the precision, recall and f1-score.

We have found that the best classification algorithm for this dataset is Random Forest. What does our forest look like? How many trees is it comprised of?

In [ ]:
'''
Disecting our Forest

Code References:
https://towardsdatascience.com/4-ways-to-visualize-individual-decision-trees-in-a-random-forest-7a9beda1d1b7
'''

# How many trees do we have?
print('Trees in our forest: %s' % len(clf.estimators_))

# Let's display them all
from sklearn.tree import plot_tree

fig = plt.figure(0, (24,14))
num_cols = 10
num_rows = 10
for i, tree in enumerate(clf.estimators_):
    plot_tree(tree, feature_names=x.columns, filled=True)
    fig.add_subplot(num_rows, num_cols, i+1)

Trees in our forest: 100

Wow, that looks like a mess. 100 trees is a lot of trees. Let's pick 1 randomly and display what it looks like.


NOTE: DO NOT RUN THIS FOR YOURSELF. IT TOOK 21 MINUTES TO RUN ON MY MACHINE.

In [ ]:
'''
Get 2 random tree from the forest and display them

Rerun this as many times as you want to view different trees
'''
import random

r = random.randint(0,101)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(15,15), dpi=300)
plot_tree(clf.estimators_[r], feature_names=x.columns, filled=True);

That is a very big tree!

Conclusion¶

From what we have seen, the Random Forest Classification Alogorithm was the best performing algorithm on our dataset, but not by much. The Decision Tree, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Naive Bayes algorithms were not that far behind. In contrast, K-Nearest Neighbors was left far behind the rest of the algorithms. Random Forest likely was the best due to the fact that it is made up of many decision trees and can handle a dataset with a lot of features well. Unlike Random Forest, K-Nearest Neighbors did not perform well because of the large amount features.
